title: A Lip-Smacking Look at Barbecue
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history and culture of barbecue: its claimed origins in indigenous cooking on Hispaniola (Tano people) and Hernando de Soto's 1540 pig roast with the Chickasaw near Tupelo, the low-and-slow method rooted in colonial pig-raising, charcoal briquettes (Ellsworth, Henry Ford's waste wood, Kingsford), the Weber kettle grill, wood flavors, dry and wet rubs, grilling versus barbecuing, regional sauces (Carolinas, Memphis, Texas, Alabama white sauce, Kansas City, Georgia), sides like Brunswick stew and mac and cheese, barbecue in politics and presidential barbecues, and barbecue's role in slavery, Jim Crow-era take-out joints, and civil rights meetings (including Auburn Avenue's Ebenezer-area restaurant Alex's Barbecue Heaven, now a Walmart). The episode closes with listener mail about the Charlottesville rally and the Vice News documentary.

segments.title: Opening banter and sushi tangent
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about vegetarians tuning out, then Josh describes a bad sushi meal in Toronto and the hole-in-the-wall sushi debate before turning to barbecue.

segments.title: Barbecue as American and global
segments.summary: They discuss barbecue as seen as quintessentially American, the barbecue belt from Virginia through the Southeast, Kansas, and Texas, and the spread of barbecue to cities like New York and San Francisco. They note barbecue exists worldwide and that its European-settler origins drew on indigenous cooking, starting with the Tano on Hispaniola.

segments.title: Defining barbecue vs. meat and three
segments.summary: They define barbecue as a noun and as slow cooking of meat over low heat for hours, distinguish it from Southern meat-and-three cafeteria cooking, and debate the purist view that barbecue must be pork, citing a 1990s Esquire article called My Pig Beats Your Cow.

segments.title: Origins of pork barbecue in the colonial South
segments.summary: The hosts explain that Southern barbecue of pork arose from colonists who let pigs forage in woods, producing tough lean meat that needed long, low cooking. They discuss the ancient history of cooking meat and a theory linking cooking to human brain growth.

segments.title: Pit cooking, turnspit dogs, and De Soto's barbecue
segments.summary: They cover medieval English turnspit dogs, the Tano method using green wood, Hernando de Soto's 1540 pig roast near Tupelo with the Chickasaw, and how pig slaughter became a community gathering. The word barbacoa is discussed as a possible Tano origin.

segments.title: Charcoal briquettes, Kingsford, and the Weber kettle grill
segments.summary: They trace the grill's evolution from wooden frames to the charcoal briquette patented by Ellsworth, the Kingsford company's origins tied to Henry Ford's wood waste, and George Stephen's 1950s kettle grill, while noting portable backyard grills predated it.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Brief sponsor and transition segment; a sponsor reference to Weber appears in the discussion.

segments.title: Wood flavors, rubs, and sauces
segments.summary: They discuss smoking woods such as hickory, mesquite, and fruit woods, advice on tasting woods, dry versus wet rubs with sweetness, savory, and spicy components, and the difference between barbecuing and grilling by time and temperature. They also cover regional sauce styles from the Carolinas, South Carolina mustard sauce, West Texas brisket, Memphis tomato-molasses sauce, and Alabama white sauce.

segments.title: Georgia and Atlanta barbecue, sides, and politics
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Georgia and Atlanta barbecue spots such as Fat Matt's Rib Shack, Fox Brothers, and Community Barbecue, typical sides like coleslaw, Brunswick stew, and baked beans, then turn to barbecue's long ties to politics, including Daniel Webster's 1836 St. Louis speech, William Henry Harrison, and Lyndon Johnson's barbecue diplomacy.

segments.title: Barbecue, slavery, Jim Crow, and civil rights
segments.summary: They explain how barbecue pit masters were often enslaved, how Jim Crow-era take-out barbecue joints began, and how barbecue restaurants served as civil rights meeting places. They discuss Alex's Barbecue Heaven in Atlanta, a King-associated spot that became a Walmart after eminent domain.

segments.title: Listener mail on Charlottesville and the Vice News documentary
segments.summary: A listener recommends the Vice News short documentary on the Charlottesville white nationalist rally, and another listener writes about the Free Speech episode and sharing it.
